abstract: Protein thermodynamic stability is a major determinant of cellular function, yet traditional methods for determining protein stability require large quantities of pure protein under idealized conditions. Here, we overcome this challenge by combining X-ray hydroxyl radical footprinting monitored by mass spectrometry (XF-MS) with chemical denaturation, to accurately measure protein thermodynamic stability. We demonstrate that XF-MS quantitatively reproduces known stability values using ~500-fold less protein than traditional spectroscopic approaches such as circular dichroism. Detection with mass spectrometry extends these measurements to heterogeneous samples demonstrated by measuring the stability of individual proteins in complex mixtures, including in cell lysate. Furthermore, by monitoring XF-MS at the level of individual peptides, we can monitor local stability and detect deviations from the typical assumed two-state unfolding behavior. This local resolution allows us to detect distinct cooperative units and assign thermodynamic values to individual structural domains within a multi-domain protein. In sum, XF-MS extends quantitative stability measurements to a broader range of proteins, environments, and levels of structural detail than previously accessible with conventional approaches.
